# Patients pay the price as Michigan healthcare systems consolidate

![A rendering of Henry Ford Hospital's \$2.2 billion expansion in Detroit, which the health system calls "Destination: Grand" (Henry Ford Health).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/djnf-data-2026/laine-cibulskis/main/docs/images/expansion.png)

![CJ Smith rests at the Ascension Providence Hospital in Southfield during a sickle cell crisis in 2024 (Cydni Elledge/Outlier Media).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/djnf-data-2026/laine-cibulskis//main/docs/images/patient.png)

::: callout-note
*Outlier Media called the disease a "poster child for medical inequity," and reported on the inability for Black adult patients to receive proper care. Ascension controls over \$39 billion in assets and 90 hospitals across the U.S. The [state allotted](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/-/media/Project/Websites/mdhhs/Public-Health-Genomics/HEMQIP/2026-Strategic-Plan-to-Address-Sickle-Cell-Disease-Across-the-Lifespan.pdf) \$5 billion to sickle cell treatment, which supported Henry Ford Hospital's new sickle cell clinic. It opened in 2024 serving 180 people at the time, according to [Outlier Media](https://outliermedia.org/sickle-cell-care-future-better-tests-detroit/). Sickle cell disease is [estimated](https://www.michigan.gov/whitmer/news/proclamations/2025/06/19/june-19-2025-sickle-cell-awareness-day) to impact 4,000 Michiganders.*
:::

Michigan hospital systems are getting bigger, but have patients paid a price for consolidation? This story will focus on the shrinking number of players in Michigan healthcare and how it has affected access to specialty care throughout the state. One example: a 2022 Michigan health care merger created a combined 22-hospital system, Corewell Health, with claims of improving patient care. 

This analysis focuses on the before and after effects of the Corewell merger on counties affected by the merger (those that have Corewell hospitals). Another distinction was also made to test health disparities between northern and southern Michigan.

Last week, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan finally reached a settlement with the University of Michigan Health (Michigan Medicine). The contract renegotiation between the two systems, which allows patients under the insurer to receive care at Michigan Medicine, had nearly failed, threatening 300,000 Detroit residents with a loss of care from one of the state's most reputable health systems. As in many industries, consolidation has taken over healthcare.

In 2023, Michigan Medicine acquired another health system as well. Still, insurance companies blame hospitals for rising costs, and insurance companies blame hospitals. This April, Michigan Medicine sang praise for the results of the 2023 merger.

But a [May KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/hospital-prices-have-risen-much-faster-for-private-insurance-than-medicare-since-2019/) study showed hospital prices are rising much faster for private insurance than Medicare since 2019. Another [KFF briefing from 2024](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/ten-things-to-know-about-consolidation-in-health-care-provider-markets/) explains that a large body of evidence points to healthcare consolidation increasing costs, but that the verdict on patient outcomes is less straightforward.

Michigan Medicine [claims](https://prod.crainsdetroit.com/health-care/whats-behind-blue-cross-michigan-medicine-contract-dispute) it should be rewarded with better contracts thanks to its quality of care and focus on specialty medicine. But how has consolidation really worked out for patients in Michigan, from their health to their pocketbooks? Especially as Detroit's hospital buildings get shinier and taller, as with Henry Ford Hospital's in-progress \$2.2 billion, 20-story [expansion](https://www.henryford.com/news/2026/05/henry-ford-hospital-construction-milestone#)?

Thanks to an insurance dispute, [nearly](https://www.detroitnews.com/story/business/2026/05/27/blue-cross-michigan-medicine-reach-deal/90274740007/) 300,000 patients lost their access to the state's premier health system thanks to an insurance dispute [in June](https://www.detroitnews.com/story/business/2026/05/06/blue-cross-tells-250000-michigan-medicine-patients-find-new-doctors/89960599007/), healthcare costs [continue to soar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12920308/) and a \$2.2 billion hospital construction project just reached [20 stories tall last month](https://www.henryford.com/news/2026/05/henry-ford-hospital-construction-milestone#): it's time explain the juxtaposition between shiny buildings and growing systems with patient struggles.

Only Michigan's specialty care is concentrated in the populous Southwest area of the state: 16 of Michigan's 83 counties reported having hospitals providing specialty care. One key note for Michigan: that care is concentrated in the south of the state, as opposed to states with more equally distributed healthcare centers like Illinois, which has a similar overall population (Chicago and UIUC in southern Illinois are two major health centers). They're very populated Michigan counties, but the spending disparity is clear, especially as more investment is brought to Detroit.

Michiganders need to know how consolidation has actually affected their access to healthcare, beyond what the pressers from healthcare companies and daily news can tell them. Additionally, the Detroit News has identified a gap in its data coverage of healthcare, in addition to a gap in its business of healthcare coverage, which is usually covered on an as-needed basis.

### Business context: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan

According to BCBS of Michigan's financial statements, published on their website, premium revenue increased by over \$1 billion from 2024 to 2025. However, financial weakness shows in a consistent operating loss, which was at a \$975 million loss in 2025. The company insures over 4 million Michiganders.

### Contextualizing the increase and possible holes

The final story would include data over time for all specialty hospitals by county, not just those reporting expenditures. Additionally, individual-hospital level data, that was noted above, will be used to pinpoint areas with mergers and hospital closures.

The story cannot claim causality, but it can show just how concentrated hospital spending is in just a few counties, and how that has changed over time as consolidation has increased. Incorporating the individual-hospital level data will help.

How common is it for other states to have specialty care concentrated in just a few areas? What about the differences in states by county-level highs? What is the best way to connect this expenditure data with patient cost data? And what will tracking hospital locations and expenditures over a longer time period show when considering larger merger dates?

### Potential sources

**Thomas Buchmueller**, University of Michigan health economist

**Bill Farmer**, healthcare advocate who co-founded the Michigan For Single Payer Healthcare grassroots organization with **Eli Rubin**

**Carl St. Amour**, Michigan Medicine's Director of Revenue, Reporting, and Payment Strategies

**Mathhew Cox**, Chief Financial Officer at Corewell Health

Founders of Michigan's New Day Foundation for Families **Michael Spehn and Gina Kell Spehn** may be able to connect me with patients receiving high-cost specialty care. New Day focuses on working with hospitals to reach patients nearing financial breaking points, especially when it comes to cancer treatment. Many board members have had personal experiences with cancer and costs as well

### More visual possibilities

County-by-county data from the Area Health Resource Files could be used to create a gradient map with a drop-down menu to show different variables for each Michigan county. There could be a scroll for change over time in different metrics such as hospital expenditures and patient outcomes.

A locator map could show detailed information about Detroit healthcare consolidation (imagine a map with points color-coded by offices owned by different entities); another locator map could also display locations of hospitals throughout the state with key expenditure points.

A collaboration with a photographer could result in a patient photo story to add a human element.

### Further reporting needs

- Academic input on the nuances of healthcare market consolidation as it relates specifically to Michigan
- Corporate and patient input
- Insurance input (private, Medicare/Medicaid)
- Continued exploration of data (direct patient costs, changes for particular hospital locations)

### First reporting steps

Kim North Shine, senior public relations representative at the University of Michigan who specializes in public health as one of her topic areas, may be able to help me get in touch with both academic and healthcare sources. Connecting with the advocacy groups mentioned above will also help kick start the reporting side of the story.

### Delivery expectations

Mid-July, about halfway though the internship, would be an ideal delivery given the need for further data analysis and the amount of reporting needed to contextualize the data.

::: callout-note
## Key terms (Source: AHFR User Guide)

**Short-term general hospitals** Hospitals that provide non-specialized care, and the majority of their patients stay for fewer than 30 days.

**Short-term non-general hospitals** Short term non-general hospitals provide specialized care, and the majority of their patients stay for fewer than 30 days.

**Long-term hospitals** Long-term hospitals may provide either non specialized or specialized care, and the majority of their patients stay for 30 or more days.

**Preventable Hospital Stays Rate** Hospitalization for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions, diagnoses usually treatable in outpatient services, suggests that the quality of care provided in the outpatient setting was not accessible. The measure may also represent a tendency to overuse emergency room and urgent care as a main source of care.
:::

::: callout-note
## Data Dictionary

| Column name | Definition |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **General Hospital** | Includes only short-term general hospitals |
| **Extra Care** | Includes short-term non-general and long-term hospitals |
| **Hospitals** | The total count of either general hospitals or extra care hospitals, depending on the frame of analysis |
| **Expenditures** | Annual hospital expenditures, separated by hospital type |
| **Expenditures per Hospital** | Annual hospital expenditures divided by the hospital count and separated by hospital type |
| **Preventable Hospital Stays Rate** | The hospital discharge rate for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions per 100,000 FFS Medicare enrollees ages 18 and older. This measure is age-adjusted |
| **Corewell County** | These counties have a Corewell hospital, sourced from Corewell's hospital locations [page](https://careers.corewellhealth.org/us/en/hospital-locations) |
| **South County** | This distinction covers the thumb, southern Michigan and southeast county designations, per Michigan State University's [distinctions](https://www.canr.msu.edu/difficult_conversations/national-and-statewide-resources/michigan-regional-resources/index). Counties are given a "0" if they fall in the upper peninsula, northern Michigan, west Michigan or central Michigan designations |
:::

### General hospitals in Michigan counties

#### 2023

```{r}
# Base table (preventable stays data not available for 2023, 2022 data is included in the AHRF 2025 data)
generalhosp23_MI <- AHRF2025_MI |>
  select(cnty_name, stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23, stgh_rptng_exp_23, medcr_ffs_prev_hosp_rate_22) |>
  rename(County = cnty_name, Hospitals = stgh_rptng_exp_23, Expenditures = stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23, "Preventable Stays Rate" = medcr_ffs_prev_hosp_rate_22) |>
  mutate(Expenditures = Expenditures*1000) |>
  mutate("Expenditures per Hospital" = (Expenditures / Hospitals)) |>
  mutate_all(~replace(., is.nan(.), 0)) |>
  arrange(desc("Expenditures per Hospital")
)

# Table for large data set analysis
gh23_MI <- generalhosp23_MI |>
  select(County, Hospitals, Expenditures, "Expenditures per Hospital", "Preventable Stays Rate") |>
  rename(hosp_gh23 = Hospitals, exp_gh23 = Expenditures, exp_per_hosp_gh23 = "Expenditures per Hospital", prevstays_22 = "Preventable Stays Rate")

```

## Analyzing Corewell v. non-Corewell change over time

### General hospitals

```{r}
# Join
gh_MI <- gh21_MI |>
  left_join(gh22_MI, by = "County") |>
  left_join(gh23_MI, by = "County") |>
  mutate("Corewell County" = case_when(
  County %in% merged_county ~ 1,
  TRUE  ~ 0
  ))

gh_MI <- gh_MI |>
  select(County,hosp_gh23, hosp_gh22, hosp_gh21, exp_per_hosp_gh23, exp_per_hosp_gh22, exp_per_hosp_gh21, prevstays_21, prevstays_22, "Corewell County") |>
  mutate(exp_per_hosp_pct_change21_22 = ((exp_per_hosp_gh22 - exp_per_hosp_gh21) / (exp_per_hosp_gh21)) * 100) |>
  mutate(exp_per_hosp_pct_change22_23 = ((exp_per_hosp_gh23 - exp_per_hosp_gh22) / (exp_per_hosp_gh22)) * 100) |>
  mutate(exp_per_hosp_pct_change21_23 = ((exp_per_hosp_gh23 - exp_per_hosp_gh21) / (exp_per_hosp_gh21)) * 100) |>
  mutate(prevstays_pct_change21_22 = ((prevstays_22 - prevstays_21) / (prevstays_22) *100))
```

```{r}
  select(hosp_gh23, hosp_gh22, hosp_gh21, exp_per_hosp_gh23, exp_per_hosp_gh22, exp_per_hosp_gh21, "Corewell County", exp_per_hosp_pct_change21_22, exp_per_hosp_pct_change22_23, exp_per_hosp_pct_change21_23) |>
```

##### Quick IL comparison

##### 2025, general hospitals in Illinois counties

```{r}
generalhosp23_IL <- AHRF2025_IL |>
  select(cnty_name,stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23, stgh_rptng_exp_23) |>
  rename(County = cnty_name, Hospitals = stgh_rptng_exp_23, Expenditures = stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23) |>
  mutate(Expenditures = Expenditures*1000) |>
  mutate("Expenditures per Hospital" = (Expenditures / Hospitals)) |>
  mutate_all(~replace(., is.nan(.), 0)) |>
  arrange(desc("Expenditures per Hospital")
)
```

##### 2025, extra care hospitals in Illinois counties

```{r}
extracare23_IL <- AHRF2025_IL |>
  select(cnty_name,stnglth_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23, stnglth_rptng_exp_23) |>
  rename(County = cnty_name, Hospitals = stnglth_rptng_exp_23, Expenditures = stnglth_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23) |>
  mutate(Expenditures = Expenditures*1000) |>
  mutate("Expenditures per Hospital" = ( Expenditures / Hospitals)) |>
  mutate_all(~replace(., is.nan(.), 0)) |>
  arrange(desc("Expenditures per Hospital")
)
```

## National comparison by state

### Short-term general hospitals

#### Total short-term general hospital expenditures by state

```{r}
stgh_23_exp_by_state <- 
  AHRF2025 |>
  select(st_name_abbrev, stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23) |>
  group_by(st_name_abbrev) |>
  summarise(stgh_23_by_state = (sum((stgh_reprtd_fac_exp_thou_23 * 1000)))
  )
```

#### Number of short-term general hospitals by state

```{r}
stgh_23_by_state <- 
  AHRF2025 |>
  select(st_name_abbrev, stgh_rptng_exp_23) |>
  group_by(st_name_abbrev) |>
  summarise(stgh_23_by_state = (sum(stgh_rptng_exp_23))) |>
  arrange(desc(stgh_23_by_state)
  )
```

#### Joining the two new data frames

```{r}
stgh_23 <-
merge(x = stgh_23_exp_by_state, y = stgh_23_by_state, by = "st_name_abbrev", .keep_all=TRUE)
```

#### Total short-term general hospital expenditures by state, per hospital in the state

```{r}
stgh_23 |>
  mutate(stgh_23_exp_by_state_ph = (stgh_23_by_state.x / stgh_23_by_state.y)) |>
  arrange(desc(stgh_23_exp_by_state_ph)
  )
```

#### Save total short term general hospital expenditures by state, per hospital in the state to use in other operations

```{r}
# Renaming
stgh_23 <-
  stgh_23 |>
    rename(
    Expenditures = stgh_23_by_state.x,
    Hospitals = stgh_23_by_state.y,
    State = st_name_abbrev
    )

```

```{r}
generalhosp23 <-
  stgh_23 |>
  select(State, Hospitals, Expenditures) |>
  mutate("Expenditures per Hospital" = Expenditures / Hospitals) |>
  arrange(desc("Expenditures per Hospital"))
```

## Summary statistics (for counties that have at least one hospital)

*My intuition was to exclude counties with zero hospitals in the summary statistics because it is a per county variable. Expenditures per hospital per county. If I'm calculating summary statistics and counties with zero hospitals are included, I would be including non-participants.*

```{r}
# generalhosp, nation
generalhosp23 |>
  filter(Hospitals != 0) |>
  summary(generalhosp23$"Expenditures per Hospital", na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Uploading data to Datawrapper for charts

### Load libraries and API key

